source: Christensen & Schunn (2007) The relationship of analogical distance to analogical function and preinventive structure: the case of engineering design
finding: In vivo study of 7 product-development meetings (medical plastics) found analogy common, and distant (between-domain) analogies nearly as common as near ones. This contrasts with Dunbar's microbiology labs, where distant analogies were rare.
numbers: 102 analogy segments in 7 transcripts (11.3 per hour, range 4-21 per transcript). 55% within-domain, 45% between-domain.
limits: One design firm, one team, one product area. Coding by hand with Dunbar's method (explicit mapping plus explicit transfer).
agent_relevance: Distant sources are not exotic in practice when the task is design. An agent doing open mode can expect about half its useful analogies to come from outside the task domain.

source: Christensen & Schunn (2007) The relationship of analogical distance to analogical function and preinventive structure: the case of engineering design
finding: Check that 'between-domain' really means low surface similarity. Within-domain analogies shared surface features (size, shape, colour, material); between-domain ones almost never did.
numbers: Sources sharing all 4 surface features: 85% of within-domain, 0% of between-domain. Sharing none: 61% of between-domain, 0% of within-domain. Mean shared features 3.82 vs 0.52, t(100)=17.21, p<.001.
limits: Only 4 surface features were coded; the authors say this is not a full list.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap, code-checkable distance measure for a source: count shared surface features. Could tag whether a retrieved analogy is near or far.

source: Christensen & Schunn (2007) The relationship of analogical distance to analogical function and preinventive structure: the case of engineering design
finding: Exemplars at hand reduce distant analogies. Segments about unsupported ideas had more analogies than segments about prototypes; the gap came entirely from between-domain analogies. Supports Ward's path-of-least-resistance and unconscious plagiarism accounts.
numbers: Share of segments with an analogy: idea vs prototype chi2(1)=7.88, p=.006; overall chi2(2)=7.96, p=.019. Segments N: idea 1,616, sketch 220, prototype 1,383. Distance x structure chi2(2)=19.26, p<.001. Fisher exact idea vs prototype p<.001, sketch vs prototype p=.019.
limits: Correlational, in one team. Sketches fell between ideas and prototypes.
agent_relevance: Showing the agent a concrete prior solution may pull it toward near, same-domain copying. Generate distant sources before showing examples. Same direction as the fixation work (06_fixation).

source: Christensen & Schunn (2007) The relationship of analogical distance to analogical function and preinventive structure: the case of engineering design
finding: Analogies serve three functions and distance depends on function. Problem-identifying analogies were mostly near; explaining analogies mostly far; problem-solving analogies mixed.
numbers: Function split: 28% identify problem, 40% solve problem, 32% explain. Distance varies with function chi2(2)=20.93, p<.001. All pairwise differences significant (identify vs solve chi2(1)=6.72, p<.01; solve vs explain 6.19, p<.02; identify vs explain 20.83, p<.001).
limits: Function coding by hand; kappa not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Far sources mainly help to explain and to seed solutions, not to find what is wrong. Use near cases for diagnosis and far cases for generating candidates.

source: Christensen & Schunn (2007) The relationship of analogical distance to analogical function and preinventive structure: the case of engineering design
finding: A far analogy that meets several constraints can still fail on one hidden constraint, and the team drops it. Example: Venetian blinds were foldable and sturdy but not water soluble.
numbers: Qualitative protocol excerpt. Other studies cited: Bearman et al. found 27% of management analogies served illustration; Dunbar found almost half of lab analogies were explanatory.
limits: Single anecdote used to illustrate, not a test.
agent_relevance: The test step after a far mapping must check every constraint, not only those that motivated the analogy. Candidate inferences need a constraint check by code or a second pass.

source: Dunbar (1995, 1997, 2001) as reported by Christensen & Schunn (2007): in vivo study of microbiology labs
finding: Second-hand only. Christensen & Schunn state that Dunbar split lab analogies into local, regional and distant, found distant ones very rare and not significant in discovery, and found between-domain analogies mostly explanatory.
numbers: No counts of Dunbar's own in this paper. Quoted facts: distant analogies 'very rare'; almost half of analogies were explanatory.
limits: I did not open Dunbar's papers (no open copy reachable this session). Treat as reported by a third party.
agent_relevance: Dunbar's result is the main caution against 'far is better'. Real scientists mostly use regional analogies (same broad field). Do not force remote sources for every problem.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text matrix reasoning, letter-string analogies and verbal analogies, zero-shot. The best humans still beat it.
numbers: Digit Matrices, humans N=40: GPT-3 above humans in generation (OR=1.88, p=.005) and multiple choice (OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8). Letter strings, humans N=57: GPT-3 above humans (OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5).
limits: Letter-string and digit tasks are near-domain and rule-based. Later challenged by counterfactual variants (see Lewis & Mitchell).
agent_relevance: Strong base ability for relational mapping inside one well-formed problem. That is not the same as finding a distant source (retrieval).

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Verbal analogies: GPT-3 at or above human level on the UCLA Verbal Analogy Test and a Sternberg & Nigro set; above average high-school SAT level. It also showed the human-like cost of semantic distance between the analogs.
numbers: Semantic-distance effect for GPT-3 on the Jones et al. set: OR=3.24, p=.0165, CI [1.24, 8.5]. Human participants were MTurk workers with at least high-school education.
limits: Verbal A:B::C:D items, not open-ended source finding.
agent_relevance: Semantic distance hurts models as it hurts people. Far mappings need more explicit help (name the relation first).

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Story analogies using Gentner et al. materials: the one place students clearly beat GPT-3. GPT-3 was significant for near analogies but not for far (cross-domain) ones.
numbers: Humans N=54 UCLA students. Combined: GPT-3 binomial p=.0005, humans t(53)=21.3. Near: GPT-3 p=.0039. Far: GPT-3 p=.065 (not significant), humans t(53)=16.7. Humans beat GPT-3 OR=0.37, p=.0003. 15 of 54 humans were right on every trial. GPT-4 preliminary: better, near perfect on near.
limits: GPT-3 only; GPT-4 results are preliminary in the supplement.
agent_relevance: The far-analogy gap is the weak point of a base model: picking the causally matched story when entities differ. A scaffold should present relations first and entities second.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed generalisation of Webb et al. Letter-string problems on permuted or symbol alphabets: humans stay high, GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 fall sharply. On the original problems models were also below humans, unlike in Webb et al.
numbers: Overall accuracy over all alphabets: humans 0.753 [0.734, 0.773] (1,876 samples, 136 Prolific participants recruited); GPT-3 0.488; GPT-3.5 0.350; GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Comprehension check: GPT-3.5 predecessor on permuted letters (n=0 alphabet) only 0.49. Alternative-rule errors: humans 38.6%, GPT-4 22%, GPT-3 5.8% of errors.
limits: Letter-string task only. Webb et al. reply that tasks in the original paper were not all on the internet.
agent_relevance: Models lean on familiar surface forms. A scaffold should not trust fluent mapping on unusual material; verify the mapping by code on the typed structure.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Reply to Lewis & Mitchell and Hodel & West. Claims Digit Matrices and letter-to-concept problems were novel and not on the web. With code execution GPT-4 reached human level on counterfactual letter strings.
numbers: GPT-4 + code execution vs humans: P=0.496 (no difference). GPT-4 alone below humans P=8.9e-13. 46% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% of human errors reported by Lewis & Mitchell.
limits: Authors of the original claim; I read the first pages and the statistics only.
agent_relevance: Offloading the mapping to executable code closes the gap. Supports our design: typed mapping checked by code, not by free generation.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis, Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Raven's matrices turned into text. Zero-shot, big models exceed the human numbers on the hardest sub-tasks; how the problem is described matters a lot. Numeric names for attributes beat random names, and splitting attributes into separate prompts helps small models most.
numbers: GPT-3 175B Center: 77.2% with numeric naming; quasi-image naming up to 28.2%; random naming up to 51.8%. Decomposition +2.8 points for GPT-3 175B; OPT 125M 22.2% to 45.6%; OPT 1.3B 47.2% to 72.0%. 2x2Grid 87.8%, 3x3Grid 93.2% with naming and decomposition, above human numbers. Chance 12.5%.
limits: Human reference taken from Zhang et al. 2019 after task training, visual format; the authors list this as a caveat.
agent_relevance: Problem encoding changes analogy accuracy by tens of points. The schema should fix a canonical encoding for mapping inputs.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (analogical prompting)
finding: Prompt the model to recall K related problems of its own and solve them, then solve the target. Beats 0-shot CoT and hand-written few-shot CoT on math, code and BIG-Bench with no labelled examples.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo: 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated exemplars 77.8. MATH GPT-3.5: 33.0 / 33.9 / 34.9 / 37.3. text-davinci-003 GSM8K: 14.8 / 50.3 / 54.0 / 61.0. PaLM2 GSM8K 60.8 / 78.2 / 80.7 / 81.7; MATH 27.1 / 29.8 / 34.3 / 34.8.
limits: The self-generated 'analogs' are mostly same-type problems (near sources), not distant ones. Gains on GPT-3.5 GSM8K are about 1 to 2 points. One model family set and a few datasets.
agent_relevance: Cheap to add as a step: ask for related solved problems before solving. It tests near analogy, not distant-source creativity.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (analogical prompting)
finding: Codeforces and BIG-Bench results. A self-written tutorial of high-level knowledge before the exemplars helps code. Diversity of exemplars and enough of them (K=3 or more) matter. Needs large models; small ones fail to produce valid exemplars.
numbers: Codeforces Acc@1 GPT-3.5-turbo-16k: 0-shot 8, CoT 9, 3-shot CoT 11, exemplars 13, knowledge+exemplars 15; GPT-4: 16, 16, 17, 17, 19. BIG-Bench GPT-3.5 first task: 66.8 / 67.6 / 68.4 / 75.2. Exemplar count GSM8K: K=1 76.1, K=3 77.8, K=5 77.3; MATH K=1 34.8, K=3 37.3. Diverse vs non-diverse exemplars 77.8/37.3 vs 75.9/35.2. With self-consistency 85.3 and 46.0.
limits: Compute cost is higher (more tokens). Few-shot CoT beats it on small models (below text-davinci-002 level).
agent_relevance: Ask for 3 diverse recalled problems plus a short principle, not 1. Do not use on weak models.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: Narrative benchmark that separates surface similarity from system (relational) similarity and near from far domain. Models do well on near analogies and badly on far ones; GPT-4 is below chance when a far analogy competes with a surface-similar distractor.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy (chance 50%) by (analogy, distractor) near/far: GPT-4 94.0, 92.5, 57.1, 29.1 (avg 68.1); GPT-3.5 88.1, 81.3, 50.4, 21.7 (avg 60.3); SBERT 84.3, 71.5, 12.6, 1.0; average of 12 models 57.3 vs humans 96.0 (98.6, 97.2, 96.8, 91.4). Human check: 2 raters on 120 items. Far analogies: models 39.6% on average vs humans 94.1%. Few-shot and CoT help.
limits: Human sample is 2 research assistants on 120 items. Benchmark is machine-built from narratives and checked by hand.
agent_relevance: Direct measurement of the core failure: surface-similar distractors beat structurally right far sources. Embedding similarity (SBERT) is worst at this. Retrieval of distant sources must not rely on plain embedding similarity.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting large language models: a case study of InstructGPT
finding: Asked InstructGPT for a source concept for a target (ACG) or an explanation of a given pair (AEG). The largest model reaches the human share of meaningful analogies on ACG; prompt wording (imperative vs question) and temperature matter a lot.
numbers: Share of generated analogies judged meaningful: NO_SRC 0.3B 1.90%, 1.3B 15.61%, 6.7B 48.29%, 175B 70.05%, human 66.67%. With source set (WSRC): 8.97, 29.05, 38.46, 53.79, human 71.88. About 1.4k generations rated; kappa 0.3-0.5 (fair to moderate).
limits: Authors warn that memorised well-known analogies may explain the scores. Low rater agreement. Not tested for novelty or distance.
agent_relevance: Scale matters sharply. A free-form 'give me an analogy' call is at best about 70% usable on a large model; filter and check each one.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining
finding: Represent a product by its purpose and its mechanism. Retrieve items with near purpose but far mechanism. These were better inspiration for ideation than surface (TF-IDF) retrieval or random items. Crowd experiment, within subjects.
numbers: 38 AMT workers; 749 ideas; 12 inspirations per condition. Seeds in all three conditions (9): good ideas 46% (N=105) analogy vs 37% random vs 30% TF-IDF, p<=.01 (liberal rule, 2 judges). Strict rule (3 judges): 38% vs 22% vs 21%. Model estimates, liberal: pr(good) 0.71 [0.48, 0.87] vs 0.28 (TF-IDF) vs 0.27 (random); strict 0.56 vs 0.16 vs 0.14.
limits: Wide confidence intervals; authors say a replication may give a smaller effect. One redesign task. Idea quality rated by crowd judges.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that a retrieval rule 'same purpose, different mechanism' beats surface similarity for creative output. Can be mimicked by asking the model for purpose and mechanism separately.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining
finding: Learned purpose and mechanism vectors find analogous product pairs better than classical text similarity. Mechanism-only and concatenated vectors beat TF-IDF, LSA and LDA at the top of the ranking.
numbers: Precision, recall at top 1%: mechanism only 0.739, 0.023; concat 0.696, 0.022; TF-IDF 0.630, 0.020; LSA 0.413; LDA 0.435. Top 25%: concat precision 0.478 vs TF-IDF 0.441. Test pairs N=2,500, trained on about 5,500; 8,500 products with 4 annotators each.
limits: Differences at larger cut-offs are small (0.44 vs 0.48). Labels made by crowd workers looking for analogies.
agent_relevance: A weak structural representation (two slots: purpose, mechanism) is enough to beat surface retrieval. Fits a typed-slot design.

source: Hope et al. (2021) Scaling creative inspiration with fine-grained functional aspects of ideas
finding: Extends the purpose-mechanism idea with parsed functional aspects and graphs over many products. In user studies the system beat strong baselines on creative search and inspiration quality.
numbers: Abstract: outperforms baselines by 50-60%. MAP 85-87% on alternative-product-use search versus 40-60% for baselines. 62% of inspirations rated useful for design-space exploration. 400 annotating workers for labels. Inter-rater agreement about 50%.
limits: I read abstract, introduction and result text only, not every experiment. Agreement is in the low range.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as the 2017 paper at larger scale: functional decomposition makes far sources findable.

source: Mitchell (2021) Abstraction and analogy-making in artificial intelligence
finding: Review argues current AI lacks human-like abstraction and analogy; benchmarks can be solved by shortcuts. Frames analogy as central to concept transfer.
numbers: Review; no single experiment figure used.
limits: Only the opening pages were scanned for this file.
agent_relevance: Background for why we score mappings on structure and do not trust fluent text.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver: are large language models creative problem solvers?
finding: 1,600+ problems that need unusual use of objects (functional fixedness). GPT-4 often gives infeasible actions. Divergent-then-convergent prompting and step-wise self-reflection reduce failures.
numbers: GPT-4: 18.9% efficient solution, 37.5% infeasible. On 180 solvable problems: self-reflect cut infeasible solutions by 9.7 points (div-conv 4.3); div-conv raised efficient solutions by 6.5 points (self-reflect 2.2). Claude 2 and Llama-2-13B did not gain from self-reflect.
limits: About fixation and creative tool use, not analogy proper. Human comparison details not extracted.
agent_relevance: Splitting generate (divergent) from check (convergent) helps; check physical feasibility explicitly.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1980) Analogical problem solving
finding: Founding experiment: Duncker's radiation problem after reading the fortress story. Most people did not use the story unless told to.
numbers: About 10% solved the radiation problem unprompted without a story; about 30% after reading the fortress story; about 75-92% after a hint to use it (recalled, uncertain).
limits: Recalled from background knowledge; not opened this session. Verify before relying on numbers.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous retrieval is the weak step, not mapping. Our agent must be told to look for sources; it will not do so by default.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Two analogous stories plus comparison produced a general schema and more transfer than one story. Basis for schema induction.
numbers: Transfer rose when two examples were compared and a summary of the principle was written (recalled; exact percentages not verified).
limits: Recalled from background knowledge; not opened this session. Verify before relying on numbers.
agent_relevance: Support for an abstract step: write the shared principle from two sources before applying it.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: Retrieval from memory is driven by surface (object) similarity, but judged soundness and usefulness are driven by structural match. People remember surface matches and rate structural ones as better.
numbers: Recalled: surface-similar stories were retrieved most often, relational matches were rated best (numbers not recalled).
limits: Recalled from background knowledge; not opened this session. Verify before relying on numbers.
agent_relevance: Explains why free recall of sources fails for far cases and why a scorer on structure is needed. Matches Sourati et al.'s below-chance far case.

source: Dunbar (1997) How scientists think: on-line creativity and conceptual change in science
finding: Four molecular biology labs recorded in vivo. Most analogies were local or regional; distant ones rare; analogies were used for explaining and for fixing experimental problems.
numbers: Recalled: large share of analogies came from the same or neighbouring organism or field. Exact counts not recalled.
limits: Recalled from background knowledge; not opened this session. Verify before relying on numbers.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: far analogies are not the main working tool of experts.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: Connectionist model of mapping by three soft constraints: structural, semantic, pragmatic. Goal relevance is included, unlike SME.
numbers: Not recalled.
limits: Recalled from background knowledge; not opened this session. Verify before relying on numbers.
agent_relevance: The pragmatic constraint (goal relevance) is a counterpoint to SME's purely structural scoring.

source: Ward (1994) Structured imagination: the role of category structure in exemplar generation
finding: People imagining alien animals mostly copied properties of familiar Earth animals (path of least resistance).
numbers: Recalled: most drawings kept standard features such as eyes and legs; numbers not recalled.
limits: Recalled from background knowledge; not opened this session. Verify before relying on numbers.
agent_relevance: Explains why default sources are near. See sibling subfield 06_fixation_and_structured_imagination.

source: Dahl & Moreau (2002) The influence and value of analogical thinking during new product ideation
finding: Analogy use in new product ideation: far (cross-domain) analogies tend to help originality, with limits on quality and with expertise; constraints matter.
numbers: Not recalled. DOI confirmed via Crossref.
limits: Recalled from background knowledge; not opened this session. Verify before relying on numbers.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: far analogies add novelty but can cut practicality.
